name: Bamoun (Pamom)
overview: Founded in 1394 by Nchare Yen, a Tikar prince from Rifoum (Mbankim), the Bamoun kingdom is ruled by a mfon surrounded by notables, servants and the royal family. Shüpamom, the language of the Mbèn subjugated by the founder, became the language of the kingdom. Fine crafts, the cult of the dead and the great Nguon festival make Foumban famous.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, open to the Hausa, Fulani, Bororo, Basaa, Ewondo, Toupouri and Nso.
Shüpamom is spoken throughout Cameroon, notably in Yaoundé, Douala, Garoua, Bertoua and in the North-West.
The Bamoun mostly marry among themselves; marrying a foreign woman, once frowned upon, is now accepted, and women more often marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The founder drove out an indigenous people in order to settle; for more than six centuries, the land has been sacred to the Bamoun.
Having come from the kingdom of Rifoum (Mbankim) via Njimom, 15 km from Foumban, the group has kept ties with these places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The mfon (king) governs with notables, servants and the royal family; women may be queens or notables, and age does not count for notability.
The palace and the chiefdoms decide; the royal decision applies.
The son inherits from his father; a prince succeeds the king.
Secret societies: the pa nda njiinə take part in the funerals of certain notables, the mutngu dispenses justice.
King Njoya already favoured alliances with other peoples.
Respect: the elder is called monge (“big brother”), and the wife does not call her husband by his name.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Formerly matrilineal and polygamous, kinship has become patrilineal under the influence of religions; the wife joins her husband's family.
The boy proved his maturity through circumcision and javelin throwing, proof of his skill as a hunter; these rites are becoming rarer.
Steps: léénəlmuə (introductory visit), ka' laam (scheduling), too ndashi (bride price), then laam (marriage).
The suitor brings cola (pɛ, fidelity), white wine or cane wine (to “bind” the marriage), oil (to make it sacred) and salt (to give it flavour).

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The la'wu, a three-day funeral wake in honour of the ancestors, is led by the head of the family.

Sacred places: the royal cemetery Gbɛtnja' at the palace, the notables' cemetery (mfɔm), the family vaults, a sacred mountain, small sacred forests (Njintout) and the seven enthronement stones of Njimom.
Birth perpetuates life and may mark the return of a forebear; death is a passage to the beyond.
Foumban is a “cemetery town”: each family buries its dead close by and consults them in times of danger, succession disputes or abuse.
Taboos: incest; forbidden meats (pork, snake, rat). The woman owes fidelity, the child obedience.
Murder, betrayal and witchcraft were the gravest offences.
Divination: water, salt, signs, and the tarantula (ŋgamsie) which chooses between two sticks, truth or lie.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: crafts, farming. Women: petty trade (bayam-sellam), sewing, embroidery.
The lands of the kingdom belong to the king; they are acquired through inheritance, purchase or gift.
Ancestral crafts, as shown by the throne of King Mbouombouo: masks, statues, statuettes and figurines, now sold.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Attire: ntieyaa, gandoura, boubou, samara (pa'ŋguŋgaa') and hat (shŭə'tú).
King Njoya recorded many medicinal recipes in a book; people still use traditional healing.
Beauty: physical and moral, elegance and cleanliness; for women, beauty, generosity and moral qualities.
Courtship: the art of speech and sweet words (“mɛmɛ”), gifts; in the woman, glances, gestures and conduct.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: kpalum, mbaya, yaya, mbijaa, mbansie, mərɛ̀ŋge, mənduu.
Instruments: zither, bullroarer (kakanduu), tam-tam (fəm), drum (mɔɔfəm), xylophone (njȧȧ), castanets (she'she').
Dances: mbinjaa at weddings, mənduu at weddings and births, kpalum at major events, mbansie and ndanjie (dance of the princes) during the Nguon.
Festivals: the Nguon, every two years (even-numbered years), and the nja, an exhibition festival currently being restored.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Nchare Yen subdued the mbèn people, whose language he adopted, which became shüpamom.
The history of the kingdom resembles that of many Bamileke chiefdoms (marriage, religion, justice).

sections.title: The names
items: Twins receive specific masculine and feminine names.
The name is given at the shieli ceremony; it can be changed once if it brings bad luck.
Customary nicknames mark social rank; Nji + name is a title of nobility, manshüt + name designates a delegated chief.
Appellatives: njimgbie (sister-in-law), ŋge ŋkuə' (brother-in-law).
The founder, Nchare Yen (“the one who walks”), was a Tikar prince.

lessons.title: Who are the Bamoun (Pamom)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bamoun (Pamom) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bamoun (Pamom) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bamoun (Pamom) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bamoun (Pamom) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bamoun (Pamom) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bamoun (Pamom) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, open to the Haoussa, Fulani, Bororo, Basaa, Ewondo, Toupouri and Nso. • Shüpamom is spoken throughout Cameroon, notably in Yaoundé, Douala, Garoua, Bertoua and in the North-West. • The Bamoun marry mostly among themselves; marrying a foreign woman, once frowned upon, is now accepted, and women more often marry outside. • The founder drove out an indigenous people in order to settle; for more than six centuries, the land has been sacred to the Bamoun. • Having come from the kingdom of Rifoum (Mbankim) through Njimom, 15 km from Foumban, the group has kept ties with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Founded in 1394 by Nchare Yen, a Tikar prince from Rifoum (Mbankim), the Bamoun kingdom is ruled by a mfon surrounded by notables, servants and the royal family. Shüpamom, the language of the Mbèn subjugated by the founder, became the language of the kingdom. Fine crafts, the cult of the dead and the great Nguon festival make Foumban famous.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bamoun (Pamom) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bamoun (Pamom)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bamoun (Pamom) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Bamoun (Pamom) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bamoun (Pamom) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Bamoun (Pamom) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The mfon (king) governs with notables, servants and the royal family; women may be queens or notables, and age does not count for notability. The palace and the chiefdoms decide; the royal decision applies. The son inherits from his father; a prince succeeds the king.

steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Bamoun (Pamom), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bamoun (Pamom)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bamoun (Pamom), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bamoun (Pamom).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bamoun (Pamom), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bamoun (Pamom).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: couscous and njapshɛ greens (pɛn njáshə), groundnut and pistachio dishes, banana dish (mbouo mbiiŋguom), dried maize dish (mbouo kusürü). • Drinks: white wine, sugar cane wine. • Men: crafts, farming. Women: small-scale trade (bayam-sellam), sewing, embroidery.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bamoun (Pamom) eat mainly couscous and njapshɛ vegetables, groundnut and pistachio dishes, mbouo mbiiŋguom, dried maize dishes. Traditional drinks: white wine, sugar cane wine. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bamoun (Pamom): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Bamoun (Pamom)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments

vocabulary.frenchText: dance of the princes at the Nguon

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Bamoun (Pamom), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Bamoun (Pamom) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Bamoun (Pamom), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Bamoun (Pamom) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: kpalum, mbaya, yaya, mbijaa, mbansie, mərɛ̀ŋge, mənduu. • Instruments: zither, bullroarer (kakanduu), tam-tam (fəm), drum (mɔɔfəm), xylophone (njȧȧ), castanets (she'she'). • Dances: mbinjaa at weddings, mənduu at weddings and births, kpalum at major events, mbansie and ndanjie (dance of the princes) during the Nguon. • Festivals: the Nguon, every two years (even-numbered years), and the nja, an exhibition festival currently being restored.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Bamoun (Pamom), traditional dances (mbinjaa, mənduu, ndanjie) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: fəm, mɔɔfəm, xylophone, zither. Festival(s): even-numbered years, nja.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Bamoun (Pamom) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Bamoun (Pamom), traditional dances (mbinjaa, mənduu, ndanjie) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: fəm, mɔɔfəm, xylophone, zither. Festival(s): even-numbered years, nja.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bamoun (Pamom)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bamoun (Pamom), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bamoun (Pamom). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bamoun (Pamom), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bamoun (Pamom). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: crafts, farming. Women: petty trade (bayam-sellam), sewing, embroidery. • The lands of the kingdom belong to the king; access is by inheritance, purchase or gift. • Ancestral crafts, as shown by the throne of King Mbouombouo: masks, statues, statuettes and figurines, now sold.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: crafts, farming. Women: petty trade (bayam-sellam), sewing, embroidery. The lands of the kingdom belong to the king; they are accessed by inheritance, purchase or gift.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bamoun (Pamom)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bamoun (Pamom)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bamoun (Pamom), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bamoun (Pamom). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bamoun (Pamom), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bamoun (Pamom). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The la'wu, a three-day funeral wake in honour of the ancestors, is led by the head of the family. • Sacred places: the royal cemetery Gbɛtnja' at the palace, the notables' cemetery (mfɔm), the family vaults, a sacred mountain, small sacred forests (Njintout) and the seven enthronement stones of Njimom. • Birth perpetuates life and may mark the return of a forebear; death is a passage to the afterlife. • Foumban is a “city-cemetery”: each family buries its dead close to it and consults them in case of danger, succession dispute or abuse. • Taboos: incest; forbidden meats (pork, snake, rat). The woman owes fidelity, the child obedience.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The la'wu, a three-day funeral wake in honour of the ancestors, is led by the head of the family. Sacred places: the royal cemetery Gbɛtnja' at the palace, the notables' cemetery (mfɔm), the family vaults, a sacred mountain, small sacred forests (Njintout) and the seven enthronement stones of Njimom.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bamoun (Pamom) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Shüpamom
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bamoun (Pamom) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bamoun (Pamom) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bamoun (Pamom) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bamoun (Pamom) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Shüpamom. • Greetings: [məshà’shə̌] = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); [Ǔjǔəmə́] = morning greeting (one person); [PǓjǔəmə́] = morning greeting (several people). • The founder, Nchare Yen (“the one who walks”), was a Tikar prince. • Nchare Yen subdued the Mbèn people, whose language he adopted, which became Shüpamom.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Shüpamom are the first steps towards communicating with the Bamoun (Pamom). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
